title: Book 18 — The fight with Irus—Odysseus warns Amphinomus—Penelope gets presents from the suitors—the braziers—Odysseus rebukes Eurymachus
paragraphs: Now there came a common tramp who wandered all over the city of Ithaca, begging for food, notorious as an incorrigible glutton and drunkard. This man had no strength or substance in him, but he was a big, hulking fellow to look at. His real name, the one his mother gave him, was Arnaeus, but the young men called him Irus because he would run errands for anyone who would send him. As soon as he arrived, he began insulting Odysseus and trying to drive him from his own house.

“Get away from this doorway, old man,” he shouted, “or you’ll be dragged out by your neck and heels! Can’t you see they’re all winking at me, wanting me to throw you out by force? I just don’t like doing it. Get up and leave on your own, or we’ll come to blows.”

Odysseus frowned at him and said, “My friend, I’m not harming you in any way. People give you plenty, and I’m not jealous. There’s room enough in this doorway for both of us, and you don’t need to begrudge me things that aren’t yours to give. You seem to be just another tramp like me, but perhaps the gods will give us better luck later. However, don’t talk too much about fighting, or you’ll anger me. Old as I am, I’ll cover your mouth and chest with blood. I’ll have more peace tomorrow if I do, because you won’t come to Odysseus’s house anymore.”

Irus grew very angry and answered, “You filthy glutton! You chatter away like an old fishwife. I have a good mind to lay both hands on you and knock your teeth out of your head like so many boar’s tusks. Get ready, then, and let these people stand by and watch. You’ll never be able to fight someone so much younger than yourself.”

This is how they insulted each other on the smooth pavement in front of the doorway, and when Antinous saw what was happening, he laughed heartily and said to the others, “This is the finest entertainment you ever saw! Heaven never sent anything like it to this house. The stranger and Irus have quarreled and are going to fight. Let’s encourage them to do it right now.”

The suitors all came up laughing and gathered around the two ragged tramps. “Listen to me,” said Antinous. “There are some goats’ stomachs down by the fire, which we’ve filled with blood and fat and set aside for supper. Whoever wins and proves himself the better man can have his pick of them. He’ll be welcome at our table, and we won’t allow any other beggar around the house at all.”

The others all agreed, but Odysseus, to throw them off the scent, said, “Sirs, an old man like me, worn out with suffering, can’t hold his own against a young one. But my demanding belly urges me on, though I know it can only end in my getting a beating. You must swear, however, that none of you will give me a foul blow to help Irus win.”

They swore as he asked, and when they had completed their oath, Telemachus spoke up and said, “Stranger, if you’re determined to settle with this fellow, you needn’t fear anyone here. Whoever strikes you will have to fight more than one person. I’m the host, and the other chiefs, Antinous and Eurymachus, both sensible men, agree with me.”

Everyone agreed, and Odysseus tucked his old rags around his waist, revealing his strong thighs, broad chest and shoulders, and mighty arms. But Athena came to him and made his limbs even stronger still. The suitors were amazed beyond measure, and one would turn to his neighbor saying, “The stranger has shown such a thigh from under his old rags that there’ll soon be nothing left of Irus.”

Irus began to feel very uneasy when he heard this, but the servants forced him forward and brought him into the open part of the court in such fear that his limbs were trembling. Antinous scolded him and said, “You swaggering bully, you should never have been born if you’re afraid of such an old, broken-down creature as this tramp. I tell you now—and it will surely happen—if he beats you and proves himself the better man, I’ll pack you off on a ship to the mainland and send you to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him. He’ll cut off your nose and ears and pull out your guts for the dogs to eat.”

This frightened Irus even more, but they brought him into the middle of the court, and both men raised their hands to fight. Then Odysseus considered whether he should strike so hard as to kill him on the spot, or give him a lighter blow that would only knock him down. In the end he thought it best to give the lighter blow, for fear the Achaeans might begin to suspect who he was. Then they began to fight. Irus hit Odysseus on the right shoulder, but Odysseus struck Irus on the neck under the ear, crushing the bones of his skull. Blood gushed from his mouth as he fell groaning in the dust, gnashing his teeth and kicking on the ground. The suitors threw up their hands and nearly died of laughter as Odysseus grabbed him by the foot and dragged him to the outer court as far as the gatehouse. There he propped him against the wall and put his staff in his hands. “Sit here,” he said, “and keep the dogs and pigs away. You’re a pitiful creature, and if you try to make yourself king of the beggars again, you’ll fare even worse.”

Then he threw his dirty old wallet, all tattered and torn, over his shoulder by its cord and went back to sit on the threshold. The suitors went inside the gallery, laughing and congratulating him. “May Zeus and all the other gods,” they said, “grant you whatever you want for putting an end to this insufferable tramp’s pestering. We’ll take him to the mainland soon, to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him.”

Odysseus took this as a good omen, and Antinous set a large goat’s stomach before him, filled with blood and fat. Amphinomus took two loaves from the bread basket and brought them to him, toasting him with a golden cup of wine. “Good luck to you, father stranger,” he said. “You’re in a bad way now, but I hope you’ll have better times ahead.”

Odysseus answered, “Amphinomus, you seem to be a man of good sense, as you well might be, considering whose son you are. I’ve heard your father spoken of well—he is Nisus of Dulichium, both brave and wealthy. They tell me you’re his son, and you appear to be a decent person. Listen, therefore, and pay attention to what I’m saying. Man is the vainest of all creatures that live on earth. As long as heaven grants him health and strength, he thinks no harm will ever come to him. Even when the blessed gods bring sorrow upon him, he bears it as he must and makes the best of it, for God Almighty gives men their daily thoughts day by day. I know all about it, for I was once a rich man and did much wrong in my stubborn pride, confident that my father and brothers would support me. Therefore let a man fear God in all things always, and accept the good that heaven may send him without vanity. Consider the shameful way these suitors are acting—see how they’re wasting the estate and dishonoring the wife of one who is certain to return someday, and soon. No, he’ll be here shortly. May heaven send you home safely before you meet him when he comes, for once he’s here, the suitors and he will not part without bloodshed.”

With these words he made a drink offering, and after drinking, he put the gold cup back into Amphinomus’s hands. Amphinomus walked away serious and bowing his head, for he sensed trouble coming. But even so he could not escape destruction, for Athena had doomed him to fall by Telemachus’s hand. So he returned to his seat where he had been before.

Then Athena put it into Penelope’s mind to show herself to the suitors, so that she might make them even more infatuated with her and win greater honor from her son and husband. She feigned a mocking laugh and said, “Eurynome, I’ve changed my mind and have a desire to show myself to the suitors, though I detest them. I’d also like to give my son a hint that he’d better have nothing more to do with them. They speak pleasantly enough, but they mean harm.”

“My dear child,” answered Eurynome, “everything you’ve said is true. Go and tell your son about it, but first wash yourself and anoint your face. Don’t go around with your cheeks covered with tears—it’s not right for you to grieve so constantly. Telemachus, whom you always prayed you might live to see grown up, already has a beard.”

“I know, Eurynome,” replied Penelope, “that you mean well, but don’t try to persuade me to wash and anoint myself, for heaven took away all my beauty the day my husband sailed away. Nevertheless, tell Autonoe and Hippodamia that I want them. They must be with me when I’m in the gallery—I won’t go among the men alone, as that wouldn’t be proper.”

At this the old woman left the room to call the maids to their mistress. Meanwhile, Athena thought of another matter and sent Penelope into a sweet sleep. She lay down on her couch and her limbs grew heavy with slumber. Then the goddess poured grace and beauty over her so that all the Achaeans would admire her. She washed her face with the divine loveliness that Aphrodite wears when she dances with the Graces. She made her taller and more commanding, and her complexion became whiter than sawn ivory. When Athena had finished all this, she departed, and the maids came in from the women’s quarters and woke Penelope with their chatter.

“What a wonderfully sweet sleep I’ve had,” she said, passing her hands over her face, “despite all my misery. I wish Artemis would let me die so sweetly right now, so I wouldn’t waste away in despair over losing my dear husband, who had every good quality and was the most distinguished man among the Achaeans.”

With these words she came down from her upper room, not alone but attended by two of her maids. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the gallery, holding a veil before her face, with a dignified maid on either side of her. When they saw her, the suitors were overwhelmed and became so desperately infatuated that each one prayed he might win her to share his bed.

“Telemachus,” she said, addressing her son, “I’m afraid you’re no longer as wise and well-behaved as you used to be. When you were younger, you had a greater sense of propriety. Now, however, though you’re grown up—and a stranger looking at you would think you were the son of a wealthy father, judging by your size and good looks—your conduct is far from what it should be. What is all this commotion that’s been going on? How could you allow a stranger to be so disgracefully mistreated? What would have happened if he had been seriously injured as a suppliant in our house? Surely this would have brought great shame on you.”

“I’m not surprised at your displeasure, dear mother,” replied Telemachus. “I understand everything and know when things aren’t as they should be, which I couldn’t do when I was younger. I can’t, however, behave with perfect propriety at all times. One after another of these wicked people keeps driving me out of my mind, and I have no one to support me. After all, though, this fight between Irus and the stranger didn’t turn out as the suitors intended, for the stranger got the better of it. I wish Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo would break the neck of every one of your suitors, some inside the house and some outside. I wish they could all be as helpless as Irus is over there by the gate of the outer court. See how his head lolls like a drunk man’s—he’s been beaten so badly that he can’t stand up or get back to his home, wherever that may be, because he has no strength left.”

This is how they talked. Then Eurymachus came forward and said, “Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, if all the Achaeans in Iasian Argos could see you at this moment, you would have even more suitors in your house by tomorrow morning, for you are the most admirable woman in the whole world, both in personal beauty and wisdom.”

Penelope replied, “Eurymachus, heaven robbed me of all my beauty, whether of face or figure, when the Argives set sail for Troy with my dear husband among them. If he were to return and look after my affairs, I would be more respected and present a better appearance to the world. As it is, I’m oppressed with care and the afflictions heaven has seen fit to heap upon me. My husband foresaw it all, and when he was leaving home, he took my right wrist in his hand. ‘Wife,’ he said, ‘not all of us will come home safely from Troy, for the Trojans fight well with both bow and spear. They’re also excellent at fighting from chariots, and nothing decides a battle’s outcome faster than that. I don’t know, therefore, whether heaven will send me back to you, or whether I might fall at Troy. Meanwhile, you look after things here. Take care of my father and mother as you do now, and even more so during my absence. But when you see our son growing a beard, then marry whomever you choose and leave this house.’ This is what he said, and now it’s all coming true. A night will come when I must submit to a marriage I detest, for Zeus has taken from me all hope of happiness. This further grief, moreover, cuts me to the very heart. You suitors are not courting me according to my country’s custom. When men court a woman they think will make a good wife and who is of noble birth, and when each is trying to win her for himself, they usually bring oxen and sheep to feast the lady’s friends, and they give her magnificent gifts, instead of eating up other people’s property without paying for it.”
This is what she said, and Odysseus was pleased when he heard her trying to get presents from the suitors and flattering them with fair words that he knew she didn’t mean.

Then Antinous said, “Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, accept as many presents as you like from anyone who will give them to you—it’s not right to refuse a gift. But we won’t go about our business or leave this place until you’ve married the best man among us, whoever he may be.”

The others applauded what Antinous said, and each sent his servant to bring his gift. Antinous’s man returned with a large and lovely dress, beautifully embroidered, with twelve beautifully made brooches of pure gold to fasten it. Eurymachus immediately brought her a magnificent chain of gold and amber beads that gleamed like sunlight. Eurydamas’s two men returned with earrings fashioned into three brilliant pendants that sparkled beautifully, while King Pisander, son of Polyctor, gave her a necklace of the finest workmanship. Everyone else brought her a beautiful present of some kind.

Then the queen went back upstairs to her room, and her maids carried the presents after her. Meanwhile the suitors turned to singing and dancing and stayed until evening came. They danced and sang until it grew dark, then brought in three braziers to give light and piled them with chopped firewood, very old and dry. They lit torches from them, which the maids held up in turns. Then Odysseus said:

“Maids, servants of Odysseus who has been absent so long, go to the queen inside the house. Sit with her and entertain her, or spin and prepare wool. I’ll hold the light for all these people. They may stay until morning, but they won’t defeat me, for I can endure a great deal.”

The maids looked at each other and laughed, while pretty Melantho began mocking him contemptuously. She was Dolius’s daughter but had been raised by Penelope, who used to give her toys and cared for her as a child. Despite all this, she showed no consideration for her mistress’s sorrows and was having an affair with Eurymachus, with whom she was in love.

“Poor wretch,” she said, “have you completely lost your mind? Go sleep in some blacksmith’s shop or public gathering place instead of chattering here. Aren’t you ashamed to open your mouth in front of your betters—so many of them too? Has the wine gone to your head, or do you always babble this way? You seem to have lost your wits because you beat that tramp Irus. Be careful that a better man doesn’t come and club you about the head until he drives you bleeding from the house.”
“Vixen,” replied Odysseus, glaring at her, “I’ll go tell Telemachus what you’ve been saying, and he’ll have you torn limb from limb.”

With these words he frightened the women, and they hurried off into the main part of the house, trembling all over, for they thought he would do as he said. But Odysseus took his position near the burning braziers, holding up torches and watching the people—brooding all the while on things that would surely come to pass.

But Athena wouldn’t let the suitors stop their insolence for even a moment, for she wanted Odysseus to become even more bitter against them. So she prompted Eurymachus, son of Polybus, to mock him, which made the others laugh. “Listen to me,” he said, “you suitors of Queen Penelope, so I can speak my mind. It’s not for nothing that this man has come to Odysseus’s house. I believe the light isn’t coming from the torches but from his own head—for his hair is completely gone, every bit of it.”

Then, turning to Odysseus, he said, “Stranger, would you work as a servant if I sent you to the countryside and saw that you were well paid? Can you build a stone wall or plant trees? I’ll feed you all year round and provide you with shoes and clothing. Will you go then? No, you won’t, because you’ve gotten into bad habits and don’t want to work. You’d rather fill your belly by going around the country begging.”

“Eurymachus,” answered Odysseus, “if you and I were to work against each other in early summer when the days are longest—give me a good scythe and take another yourself, and let’s see which of us lasts longer or mows stronger, from dawn to dark when there’s grass to cut. Or if you want to plow against me, let’s each take a yoke of tawny oxen, well-matched and of great strength and endurance. Put me in a four-acre field and see whether you or I can cut a straighter furrow. If war broke out today, give me a shield, a couple of spears, and a helmet that fits well on my temples—you’d find me in the front ranks and would stop your jokes about my belly. You are insolent and cruel and think yourself a great man because you live in a small world, and a bad one at that. If Odysseus returns to reclaim his property, his house’s doors are wide, but you’ll find them narrow when you try to escape through them.”

Eurymachus was furious at all this. He scowled and cried, “You wretch, I’ll soon pay you back for daring to say such things to me, and in public too! Has the wine gone to your head, or do you always babble like this? You seem to have lost your wits because you beat that tramp Irus.” With this he grabbed a footstool, but Odysseus sought protection at Amphinomus of Dulichium’s knees, for he was afraid. The stool hit the cupbearer on his right hand and knocked him down. The man fell flat on his back with a cry, and his wine jug fell ringing to the ground. The suitors in the covered gallery were now in an uproar, and one would turn to his neighbor saying, “I wish the stranger had gone somewhere else—bad luck to him for all the trouble he causes us. We can’t allow such disturbance over a beggar. If such poor judgment prevails, we’ll have no more pleasure at our feast.”

At this Telemachus stepped forward and said, “Sirs, are you mad? Can’t you handle your food and drink properly? Some evil spirit has possessed you. I don’t wish to drive any of you away, but you’ve had your dinner, and the sooner you all go home to bed, the better.”

The suitors bit their lips and marveled at his bold speech, but Amphinomus, son of Nisus, who was son of Aretias, said, “Let’s not take offense—that’s reasonable, so let’s not argue. Don’t let us harm the stranger or any of Odysseus’s servants. Let the cupbearer go around with the drink offerings so we can make them and go home to rest. As for the stranger, let’s leave Telemachus to deal with him, since he has come to his house.”

This is what he said, and his words pleased them well. So Mulius of Dulichium, Amphinomus’s servant, mixed them a bowl of wine and water and passed it around to each man in turn. They made their drink offerings to the blessed gods, and after making their offerings and drinking as each desired, they went their separate ways, each to his own home.
